word_order: SVO — Subjects normally precede verbs and objects follow them (e.g. 'Steve Jobs unveiled the device' in sample 11).
register: edited written expository/encyclopedic/news prose (formal, published informational text).
clause_boundary_signals: coordinating conjunctions linking independent clauses (and, but)
subordinating conjunctions introducing dependent clauses (although, if)
relative pronouns introducing relative clauses (which, that)
complementizers/infinitival markers introducing clausal complements (that, to)
non_boundary_traps: parenthetical modifiers set off by commas (media/location tags like 'live on television')
fronted prepositional or temporal adjuncts that look like separate clauses (For over a thousand years, Around 60 cases)
infinitival 'to' phrases that are complements of verbs rather than new clauses (to appoint, to have)
unstable_prefix_signals: sentence-initial subordinators or contrastive adverbials after which attachment is undecided (Although, While)
initial temporal/prepositional adjuncts whose scope may be local or sentential (For over a thousand years, After the war)
single-word focusers/restrictors that don't determine clausehood on their own (Only, Of course)
notes_for_prompt_writer: Basic clause order is S–V–O and verbs (including auxiliaries/modals) precede main verbs. Embedded clauses commonly begin with complementizers, subordinators or relative pronouns. Fronted adverbials and parenthetical modifiers are frequent and often comma-marked, and infinitival 'to' phrases serve as verb complements rather than independent clauses.
